title: Navigating ovarian cancer at age 35 through self-advocacy
summary: Diagnosed with ovarian cancer at 35, Meighan's story highlights the power of self-advocacy, early detection, and trusting your instincts.
body_markdown:
When Meighan noticed something didn't feel right, she trusted her instincts. In January 2022, just weeks after recovering from COVID-19, she felt a hard spot in her abdomen during a workout. Having experienced years of infertility and multiple ectopic pregnancies, Meighan initially assumed these new symptoms might be related.


Instead, a trip to the emergency room revealed something unexpected: a 16-centimeter mass on her left ovary.


"I knew something wasn't right with my body," Meighan said. "But I definitely was not prepared for what happened next."


## Turning professional knowledge into personal advocacy


At the time, Meighan, a Labcorp regional manager based in South Carolina, had already spent more than a decade working in the laboratory industry. That experience immediately influenced how she approached the situation.


Meighan was just 35 years old when the mass was discovered. Though ovarian cancer risk increases as you get older, it’s still possible to develop[ovarian cancer at any age](https://ocrahope.org/news/can-you-get-ovarian-cancer-at-any-age/) .


Drawing on her knowledge of women’s health and diagnostic testing, Meighan wanted her care team to have as much information as possible before making treatment decisions. She knew it was especially important to ask questions and advocate for herself throughout the diagnostic process.


"From the moment they discovered the mass, my mind immediately went into, 'What lab tests do I need to help with the diagnosis?'" she recalled. "Lab test results are a critical piece of any patient's diagnosis."


Her OB-GYN planned to order a[CA-125 test](https://ocrahope.org/for-patients/gynecologic-cancers/ovarian-cancer/ca-125/) , a blood test that measures a protein that can be elevated in some people with ovarian cancer. While helpful, CA-125 alone does not provide a complete picture.


Because of her background in women's health diagnostics, Meighan asked her provider about an additional test:[ROMA®, or the Risk of Ovarian Malignancy Algorithm](https://www.labcorp.com/tests/140045/ovarian-malignancy-risk-roma) .[ROMA](https://www.aafp.org/afp/2023/0300/diagnostic-tests-ovarian-cancer) combines the results of two biomarkers, CA-125 (the same protein that Meighan’s OB-GYN had already planned to order) and HE4 (another protein that can be associated with ovarian cancer risk), along with menopausal status, to help assess the likelihood that an ovarian mass may be malignant. The test is intended to support clinical evaluation and help determine whether referral to a gynecologic oncologist may be appropriate.


"Had I not had knowledge of the lab industry and known about ROMA testing, my outcome would have been very different," Meighan said.


## The result that changed her care path


Meighan's experience demonstrated why additional information can matter.


Her CA-125 result fell within the normal reference range. On its own, that result may not have immediately raised concern. However, her HE4 level was elevated, and when combined with her premenopausal status through the ROMA calculation, the results suggested a significantly increased likelihood of ovarian malignancy.


Those results prompted her OB-GYN to refer her to a gynecologic oncologist before surgery. That referral proved critical; following surgery to remove her tumor, Meighan learned she had ovarian cancer. Her tumor weighed eight pounds, and her treatment ultimately included additional, extensive surgery and 18 rounds of chemotherapy.


Yet there was encouraging news. Her cancer was diagnosed at Stage 1, meaning it had remained confined to the ovary and had not spread elsewhere.


"My oncologist told me it had been many years since he had seen ovarian cancer at Stage 1," she said. Since it often does not cause symptoms until it’s more advanced,[ovarian cancer is hard to find early](https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/ovarian-cancer/detection-diagnosis-staging.html) .


Today, Meighan has no evidence of disease and continues routine monitoring.


## A new perspective on laboratory medicine


Before her diagnosis, Meighan already understood the importance of laboratory testing. Going through her ovarian cancer diagnosis gave her a deeper appreciation for the role that lab testing can play in critical healthcare decisions and outcomes.


"It gave me a sense of responsibility to make sure providers are educated and have access to the information and tools they need,” she said.


Her experience also reinforced the human side of every test result. "We talk about risk assessments, results, and numbers," she shared. "But understanding that there's a real person on the other end of these tests is so important.”


She saw firsthand how the right test at the right time can help support clinical decisions and influence a patient’s care journey. Today, that perspective shapes the conversations she has with healthcare providers.


## A message for patients: Trust yourself


Looking back, Meighan hopes her story encourages others to listen to their bodies and advocate for their health.


"We know our bodies better than anybody," she said. "When we notice something's not right, it's definitely important to get it checked."


She also encourages patients facing a possible cancer diagnosis to find a healthcare team they trust, ask questions, and lean on their support systems.


"Don't lose hope," she said. "There are so many innovative treatment options available now."


For Meighan, the experience transformed a professional passion into a personal mission.


"Knowledge is empowering," she said. "Knowing what questions to ask can make all the difference."


*Meighan Stacey is an employee of Labcorp. No compensation or remuneration of any kind was paid in connection with this story.*
